notes: Ruling slot 22 = Guardia Nacional under Torrijos; coalition slot 13 = the civilian Provisional Government Junta (Lakas/Sucre) installed after the December 1969 counter-coup. The failed December plotters sit in 0. Panameñista Party (Arnulfistas) in 20 per MD; Acción Comunal as its ultranationalist root in 21. All parties dissolved by the junta since 1969.

0.name: Los Coroneles de Diciembre
0.text:
Los Coroneles de Diciembre are the officers who tried to depose Omar Torrijos on 15 December 1969 while he was abroad in Mexico, led by colonels Amado Sanjur and Ramiro Silvera. Torrijos flew back to David, rallied the Chiriquí garrison and reversed the coup within a day. On 1 January 1970 the plotters are under arrest or in exile and their sympathisers are being purged.

They stand for a conservative, firmly pro-American Guardia, alarmed by Torrijos's populist turn and his flirtation with the left. They want order, the canal status quo and close ties with the US Southern Command. Their leverage lies in surviving loyalties in the officer corps and among American contacts in the Canal Zone.

1.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano de Panamá
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Party of Panama was founded in 1960 by young Catholic professionals seeking an alternative to the oligarchic parties and the Arnulfista movement. Like every party it was dissolved by the Guardia Nacional after the October 1968 coup, and on 1 January 1970 it survives as an underground network of lay activists.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching and the Christian Democrats of Chile and Venezuela, it calls for a return to constitutional rule, honest elections, cooperatives and a dignified, negotiated settlement on the Canal. It is anti-communist but critical of military rule. Its base is the Catholic middle class of Panama City and the universities.

2.name: Partido Liberal Nacional
2.text:
The National Liberal Party is the historic party of the Panamanian elite, which has dominated government for most of the republic's history. Its candidate David Samudio, backed by President Marco Aurelio Robles, lost the 1968 election to Arnulfo Arias. Dissolved after the coup, on 1 January 1970 its leaders are in exile, retired or quietly bargaining with the junta.

It stands for constitutional liberalism, free trade, the service economy of the Canal and the transit routes, and close cooperation with Washington within negotiated canal reforms. Its base lies among merchant families, professionals and provincial notables, and its leverage rests on wealth, newspapers and old patronage networks.

3.name: Confederación de Trabajadores de la República de Panamá
3.english: Confederation of Workers of the Republic of Panama
3.native_full: Confederación de Trabajadores de la República de Panamá
3.text:
The Confederation of Workers of the Republic of Panama is the country's main non-communist trade union centre, founded in the 1950s and affiliated to the inter-American free trade union network. On 1 January 1970 it operates under the watchful eye of the Guardia Nacional, which has banned the parties but courts organised labour.

It seeks a modern labour code, collective bargaining, social security and fair treatment for Panamanians working in the Canal Zone. Moderate and anti-communist, it is willing to cooperate with the junta in exchange for reforms. Its strength lies among transport, port and service workers in Panama City and Colón.

4.name: Partido del Pueblo de Panamá
4.text:
The People's Party of Panama is the country's communist party, founded in 1930 as the Communist Party and renamed in 1943. Outlawed for long periods, it was driven underground again after the 1968 coup; on 1 January 1970 it is led by Rubén Darío Souza and watches Torrijos's populist turn with cautious interest.

It follows the Soviet line and a united-front strategy: national sovereignty over the Canal, removal of US bases, agrarian reform and trade-union rights. It has influence among students, teachers, banana workers in Bocas del Toro and Chiriquí, and intellectuals. Its leverage lies in organisation and in the regime's search for allies on the left.

5.name: Federación de Estudiantes de Panamá
5.text:
The Federation of Students of Panama is the national student organisation founded in 1943 and hardened by the January 1964 riots, when students died trying to raise the Panamanian flag in the Canal Zone. After the 1968 coup the University of Panama was closed and purged; on 1 January 1970 its radicals mourn Floyd Britton, who died in the Coiba island prison in November 1969.

The federation mixes Marxist, Guevarist and nationalist ideas, demanding full sovereignty over the Canal, the end of US bases and social revolution. Its leverage lies in its power to mobilise the youth of Panama City and in the symbolism of the martyrs of 1964.

6.name: Los Soberanistas del Cuartel
6.text:
Los Soberanistas del Cuartel are the hardline nationalist officers of the Guardia Nacional who regard the American Canal Zone as an occupation and the 1903 treaty as a national humiliation. Marked by the 1964 flag riots, on 1 January 1970 they rally around Torrijos after the failed December counter-coup and push him toward confrontation with Washington.

They want the Canal Zone abolished, US bases removed and the canal under the Panamanian flag, by pressure if negotiations fail. Socially conservative and contemptuous of civilian politicians, they are willing to seek arms, diplomatic backing and trade from the Eastern bloc and the Third World. Their leverage lies in command posts and patriotic fervour.

7.name: El G-2
7.text:
El G-2 is the intelligence section of the Guardia Nacional, the eyes and ears of the regime born in the 1968 coup. Its rising figure is Manuel Antonio Noriega, the officer in Chiriquí whose loyalty during the December 1969 counter-coup secured Torrijos's return and who is now on his way to heading military intelligence.

The G-2 watches students, Arnulfistas, old politicians and unionists, runs informers and handles prisoners sent to Coiba island. Its men value power over ideology and cultivate Cuban and other foreign services as well as the Americans. Its leverage lies in files, fear and direct access to the commander.

8.name: Los Libaneses de la Zona Libre
8.english: Los Libaneses de la Zona Libre
8.native_full: Los Libaneses de la Zona Libre
8.text:
Los Libaneses de la Zona Libre is a small community of Lebanese Shia merchants from southern Lebanon who trade in the Colón Free Zone and the shops of Colón and Panama City. On 1 January 1970 they pray in private homes and follow the work of Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council was founded in Beirut in 1969.

They favour a modern, educated and politically moderate Shia identity, mutual aid and community pride, and stay out of Panamanian politics while keeping good terms with the authorities. Their influence rests on commerce, remittances and family networks linking Colón with Beirut and West Africa.

9.name: Los Discípulos de Nayaf
9.text:
Los Discípulos de Nayaf is a tiny group of young Lebanese Shia shop assistants and students in Colón who pass around pamphlets and recorded sermons from the seminaries of Najaf. On 1 January 1970 they are unknown outside their own families and meet quietly after closing time.

They are drawn to the teaching of the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini on Islamic government, which calls for jurists to rule in place of kings. They reject both American and Soviet models, resent the American presence in the Canal Zone and see Israel and the Shah as enemies. Their leverage is negligible beyond devotion and clerical links abroad.

10.name: Los Mercaderes del Gujarat
10.text:
Los Mercaderes del Gujarat are the Sunni Muslim families of Indian origin, mostly from Gujarat, who run textile, electronics and import businesses in Panama City and Colón. On 1 January 1970 they form the core of Panama's small Muslim community, meeting for prayer in rented halls and dreaming of a proper mosque.

Their Islam is conservative, quietist and devotional, centred on family, charity and religious education rather than politics. They respect the authorities, avoid controversy and keep ties with religious institutions in South Asia and Arabia. Their leverage lies in their commercial weight in the transit economy and good relations with every government.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
Los Estudiantes del Califato is a handful of Palestinian and Jordanian traders and students in Colón who have come into contact with Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. On 1 January 1970 they meet as a private study circle with no public presence.

They regard every existing state as illegitimate and call for the restoration of a single caliphate for all Muslims. Hostile to Israel, the United States and Soviet atheism alike, they reject elections and party politics. Their only assets are conviction and contact with the party's cells in the Middle East and Europe.

12.name: Los Hermanos del Istmo
12.text:
Los Hermanos del Istmo is a circle of devout Arab Muslim merchants in Colón and Panama City who sympathise with the Muslim Brotherhood of Hasan al-Banna. On 1 January 1970 it organises Quran lessons for children, charity for the refugees of the 1967 war and readings of Sayyid Qutb.

It calls for the moral renewal of society through preaching, education and charity, and hopes for Islamic government achieved by gradual, lawful means. It opposes Zionism, Western materialism and communist atheism. Its leverage lies in welfare networks and solidarity collections for Palestine within the Arab community of the Free Zone.

13.name: Junta Provisional de Gobierno
13.text:
The Provisional Government Junta is the civilian face of military rule. After the failed December 1969 counter-coup, Torrijos replaced Colonel José María Pinilla with Demetrio Basilio Lakas, an engineer and former head of the Social Security Fund, as president of the junta, with Arturo Sucre as his partner. On 1 January 1970 it governs by decree without a legislature.

Its ministers and planners are technocrats who favour state-led development, agrarian reform, banking and free-zone expansion, and a tough but negotiated line on the Canal. It avoids alignment with either bloc. Its leverage lies in the administration and Torrijos's trust, but every real decision passes through the Guardia command.

14.name: Arquidiócesis de Panamá
14.text:
The Archdiocese of Panama has been led since 1969 by Archbishop Marcos Gregorio McGrath, a leading voice of the reforming Latin American bishops who met at Medellín in 1968. On 1 January 1970 the Church is the only national institution besides the Guardia that keeps real independence from the junta.

It preaches social justice, rural cooperatives and the dignity of the poor, while defending public morality and religious education. It supports Panamanian sovereignty over the Canal but urges dialogue and respect for human rights. Its influence reaches parishes in the interior provinces, Catholic schools, lay movements and priests working with peasants in Veraguas.

15.name: Los Rabiblancos
15.text:
Los Rabiblancos, the white-tailed ones, is the popular name for the handful of intermarried families who have run Panama's commerce, banking, land and politics since independence in 1903. On 1 January 1970 they have lost direct control of the state to the Guardia Nacional but still own the newspapers, the big firms and the cattle estates.

They favour free enterprise, the transit and service economy, low taxes and close ties with the United States and its Canal Zone. They fear Torrijos's agrarian reform and populism yet hope to buy influence with the junta. Their leverage lies in capital, foreign bank accounts and family connections throughout the old parties.

16.name: Asociación Panameña de Ejecutivos de Empresa
16.native_full: Asociación Panameña de Ejecutivos de Empresa
16.text:
The Panamanian Association of Business Executives is a forum of managers and professionals founded in 1958 to promote modern management and free enterprise. On 1 January 1970 it is one of the few civic bodies still speaking openly on economic policy under the junta.

It champions private initiative, an open economy, the Colón Free Zone, an international banking centre and limits on state intervention. Pro-American in economic orientation, it nonetheless supports a fairer canal treaty. Its members are younger, technocratic businessmen rather than old landed families, and its leverage lies in expertise and influence over the regime's economic planners.

17.name: Congreso General Kuna
17.text:
The Kuna General Congress is the traditional assembly of the Kuna people of the San Blas archipelago, whose autonomy was won in the 1925 revolution and secured by the 1953 law establishing their comarca. On 1 January 1970 its sailas, the village chiefs, still govern communal life on the islands and the coastal forest.

It defends collective land rights, the forest and the coral reefs, and the right to manage tourism and fishing by Kuna rules. Wary of outsiders, settlers and logging companies, it negotiates with whichever government holds power in Panama City. Its leverage lies in unity, the memory of 1925 and international sympathy.

18.name: Los Asentamientos Campesinos
18.text:
Los Asentamientos Campesinos are the peasant settlements organised under the agrarian reform that Torrijos launched in 1969, when the Guardia began handing idle estates to collective farms in the interior. On 1 January 1970 the settlers of Veraguas, Coclé and Chiriquí are becoming a new political base for the regime.

They demand land, credit, roads, schools and protection from the cattle barons, and they look to the state rather than to the old parties. Their outlook is agrarian socialism without Moscow, a Panamanian road between the blocs. Their leverage lies in their numbers and in Torrijos's personal attachment to the countryside.

19.name: La Línea China
19.text:
La Línea China is the Maoist wing of the Panamanian left, formed among students and young teachers who broke with the People's Party after the Sino-Soviet split. On 1 January 1970 it is scattered and clandestine after the post-coup repression, with some sympathisers drawn to the brief guerrilla attempts in the mountains of Chiriquí.

It condemns the People's Party's courtship of the junta as revisionism and preaches people's war to drive the Americans from the Canal Zone. It looks to Beijing rather than Moscow. Its leverage lies in student militancy and in the anger of a generation that lived through 1964.

20.name: Partido Panameñista
20.text:
The Panameñista Party is the populist movement of Arnulfo Arias Madrid, three times president and three times overthrown, most recently by the Guardia Nacional on 11 October 1968 after eleven days in office. On 1 January 1970 Arias lives in exile in the United States while his supporters resist the junta, some through brief guerrilla actions in Chiriquí.

Arnulfismo combines fervent nationalism, the slogan 'Panama for the Panamanians', social welfare and hostility to both the old oligarchy and the Guardia. It commands the loyalty of the poor of the cities and the interior and remains the largest political following in the country, which is its leverage.

21.name: Acción Comunal
21.text:
Communal Action is the nationalist society founded in 1923 that seized power in the coup of January 1931 and launched the career of Arnulfo Arias. In 1970 its old members and their heirs form a hard ultranationalist core, revered as the founders of panameñismo and faithful to the exclusionary ideas of the 1941 Constitution.

They preach the supremacy of the Hispanic Panamanian nation, hostility to West Indian and Asian immigrants, Catholic order and an authoritarian state above parties. They despise both the oligarchy and the communists. Their leverage lies in nationalist mystique and networks within the Arnulfista movement and the professions.

22.name: Guardia Nacional
22.text:
The National Guard is Panama's only armed force and, since the coup of 11 October 1968, its ruler. Its commander, General Omar Torrijos Herrera, has just defeated the December 1969 counter-coup and stands unchallenged at the head of the regime. Parties are dissolved, the Assembly is closed and the junta answers to the general staff.

Torrijismo promises a revolution from the barracks: agrarian reform, labour rights, national integration and, above all, full sovereignty over the Canal through new treaties with Washington. The Guardia is nationalist and populist but pragmatic, keeping American training ties while courting the Third World. Its leverage is total control of arms, police and administration.

23.name: Los Borbónicos del Casco Viejo
23.text:
Los Borbónicos del Casco Viejo are a small Hispanist circle of Panama City notables, priests and scholars who cherish the walled colonial city and the memory of the Spanish Crown that ruled the isthmus for three centuries. On 1 January 1970 they gather in clubs and lay brotherhoods without any political organisation.

They admire Franco's 1969 choice of Juan Carlos de Borbón as heir, see hierarchy and faith as the cure for caudillismo and party chaos, and celebrate Panama's Hispanic heritage over American influence. Their influence is purely cultural, exercised through essays, ceremonies and family prestige.
